lessons.title: Energy, Work Done and Power
lessons.description: Mechanical work, gravity at different heights, work done by friction, KE and GPE conservation, and power.
lessons.content_html:
Work Done

When a force causes an object to move, energy is transferred from one store to another. The amount of energy transferred in this way is called work done. The equation is:

$$W = F \times d$$

Where \(W\) is work done in joules (J), \(F\) is the force in newtons (N), and \(d\) is the distance moved in the direction of the force in metres (m). One joule is the work done when a force of one newton moves an object one metre.

Key Fact

Work done equals energy transferred: \(W = Fd\). If the force is perpendicular to the direction of motion, no work is done — for example, the normal contact force on a horizontally sliding object does no work because it acts vertically.

A common exam application is work done against friction. When an object slides across a rough surface, friction transfers energy from the kinetic energy store to the thermal energy store of the surface and the object — both warm up slightly.

A crate is dragged 12 m across a warehouse floor against a constant friction force of 40 N. How much work is done against friction?

\(W = F \times d = 40 \times 12 = 480\) J

All 480 J is transferred to the thermal energy store of the crate and floor — they become slightly warmer. This energy is dissipated and cannot easily be recovered.

Kinetic Energy

Kinetic energy (KE) is stored in any moving object. The equation is:

$$E_k = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2$$

Where \(E_k\) is kinetic energy in joules, \(m\) is mass in kilograms, and \(v\) is speed in metres per second. Notice that doubling the speed quadruples the kinetic energy — this is why high-speed impacts are so much more destructive than low-speed ones.

Gravitational Potential Energy

Gravitational potential energy (GPE) depends on the mass, height, and gravitational field strength of the location:

$$E_p = mgh$$

Where \(E_p\) is GPE in joules, \(m\) is mass in kg, \(g\) is gravitational field strength (10 N/kg at Earth's surface), and \(h\) is height above a chosen reference point in metres. Note that \(g\) is different on the Moon, Mars, or other planets — always check the value given in a question.

Key Fact

On Earth, gravitational field strength \(g = 10\) N/kg. As an object falls, GPE decreases and, if there is no air resistance, KE increases by exactly the same amount — total mechanical energy is conserved.

Conservation of Energy

The conservation of energy principle states that the total energy in a closed system remains constant. In practice, some energy is always dissipated as thermal energy due to friction or air resistance — but the total is never lost, only spread out.

A classic example is a falling object. At the top of its path, the object has maximum GPE and zero KE. As it falls, GPE converts to KE. Just before hitting the ground, nearly all GPE has become KE (ignoring air resistance). This gives us the useful shortcut: \(mgh = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2\), which can be used to find the speed of a falling object without knowing the time of fall.

A cyclist and bike have a combined mass of 80 kg. They start from rest at the top of a smooth hill 5 m high. What is their speed at the bottom? (g = 10 N/kg)

Loss in GPE = gain in KE (smooth ramp, so no energy lost to friction):
\(mgh = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2\)
\(80 \times 10 \times 5 = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 80 \times v^2\)
\(4000 = 40v^2\)
\(v^2 = 100\)
\(v = 10\) m/s

Note that mass cancels — the speed at the bottom is independent of how heavy the cyclist is.

Efficiency

Efficiency measures how well a device converts energy into a useful form. No real device is 100% efficient — some energy is always wasted, usually as thermal energy or sound.

$$\text{efficiency} = \frac{\text{useful energy output}}{\text{total energy input}}$$

Multiply by 100 for a percentage. An electric motor with efficiency 0.75 converts 75% of electrical energy into kinetic energy; the remaining 25% is dissipated as heat in the windings and bearings.

Power

Power is the rate at which work is done or energy is transferred:

$$P = \frac{E}{t} \quad \text{or equivalently} \quad P = \frac{W}{t}$$

Where \(P\) is power in watts (W), \(E\) (or \(W\)) is energy in joules, and \(t\) is time in seconds. One watt equals one joule per second. A machine with a power of 500 W transfers 500 J every second.

Key Fact

There is a second power equation useful when a steady force moves at constant velocity: \(P = Fv\), where \(F\) is force in newtons and \(v\) is speed in m/s. This is derived by combining \(P = W/t\) with \(W = Fd\): since \(d/t = v\), it follows that \(P = Fv\).

A car engine provides a constant driving force of 1800 N while the car travels at a steady speed of 25 m/s. Calculate the power output of the engine.

\(P = Fv = 1800 \times 25 = 45\,000\) W = 45 kW

At steady speed, the driving force equals the resistive forces (air resistance + friction), so this 45 kW is entirely used to overcome resistance.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For calculate questions on energy and power, always write the equation first, substitute values with units, and give your final answer to 2–3 significant figures with the correct unit. A common error is forgetting to square the speed in \(E_k = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2\) — the squaring is not optional. For 4-mark explain questions linking work done to energy transfer, pair each step with its consequence: "the force does work on the object because it moves through a distance, so energy transfers from the chemical store of the fuel to the kinetic store of the object." For 6-mark extended responses, reference specific energy stores (kinetic, gravitational potential, thermal) rather than vague terms like 'energy.'
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Work done = force × distance (\(W = Fd\)); work done equals energy transferred. One joule is one newton-metre.
  • Kinetic energy \(E_k = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2\); gravitational potential energy \(E_p = mgh\). When an object falls freely, GPE converts to KE with no net loss.
  • Power \(P = E/t\) (rate of energy transfer, in watts). The alternative form \(P = Fv\) is used when force and constant speed are given.

lessons.title: Forces and Their Effects: Moments, Levers and Gears
lessons.description: Vector and scalar quantities, free-body diagrams, moments, levers, gears and balanced beams.
lessons.content_html:
Scalars and Vectors

Physical quantities are classified as either scalar or vector. Scalars have magnitude only; vectors have both magnitude and direction. This distinction matters whenever you add or resolve forces — you must account for direction, not just size.

Key Fact

Scalar examples: speed, mass, temperature, distance, energy. Vector examples: force, velocity, acceleration, displacement, momentum. Force is always a vector — direction is essential when drawing and analysing forces.

Free-Body Diagrams

A free-body diagram shows all forces acting on an object as labelled arrows. Each arrow starts at the object (or its centre of mass) and points in the direction of that force. Arrow length is drawn proportional to force magnitude. Common forces include weight (downward), normal contact force (perpendicular to surface), friction (opposing motion), and tension (along a string or rope).

If the arrows on a free-body diagram all balance — equal and opposite in every direction — the object is in equilibrium. This means it is either stationary or moving at constant velocity.

Step 1: Identify the object in isolation. Step 2: Draw all forces as arrows acting on that single object — not forces the object exerts on other things. Step 3: Label each force with its name and magnitude if known. Step 4: Check for balance: if the vector sum of all forces is zero, the object is in equilibrium; if not, calculate the resultant force using scale or trigonometry.

A Newton-meter (spring balance) is the instrument used to measure force. It works by measuring the extension of a spring and converting this to a force reading using Hooke's law.

Turning Effect and Moments

A force can cause an object to rotate about a fixed point called the pivot (or fulcrum). The turning effect of a force is called its moment:

$$M = F \times d$$

Where \(M\) is the moment in newton-metres (N m), \(F\) is the force in newtons, and \(d\) is the perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action of the force in metres. Perpendicular is critical — if the force is not applied at 90° to the lever arm, only the perpendicular component creates a moment.

Key Fact

The principle of moments states that for an object in rotational equilibrium, total clockwise moments = total anticlockwise moments about any pivot.

A child of weight 300 N sits 2 m from the pivot of a see-saw. Where must a second child of weight 400 N sit on the opposite side to balance it?

Clockwise moment = anticlockwise moment
\(400 \times d = 300 \times 2\)
\(400d = 600\)
\(d = 1.5\) m

The 400 N child must sit 1.5 m from the pivot on the opposite side. A heavier person sits closer to the pivot to exert the same moment as a lighter person further away.

Centre of Mass

The centre of mass is the point through which an object's weight effectively acts. For a uniform, symmetrical object — such as a ruler — the centre of mass is at the geometric centre. For irregular objects, it can be found by suspending the object from different points and drawing the plumb-line; the centre of mass is where the lines intersect.

An object will topple if its centre of mass moves outside its base. Wide, low objects (a racing car) are more stable; tall, narrow objects (a double-decker bus on a slope) are less stable. Lowering the centre of mass or widening the base increases stability.

Levers

A lever is a rigid bar that can rotate about a pivot. It uses the principle of moments to provide a mechanical advantage — a small effort force applied at a large distance from the pivot can balance (or exceed) a large load force applied closer to the pivot.

Real-world levers include: a crowbar (pivot at one end, effort at the other end, load near the pivot), a wheelbarrow (pivot at the wheel, load in the bucket, effort at the handles), and a pair of scissors (the pivot is the central bolt; the effort is the handle, the load is the material being cut).

Gears

Gears are toothed wheels that mesh and rotate together. They transmit a turning force (torque) from one axle to another. The key rule is: when a smaller gear drives a larger gear, the larger gear turns more slowly but with a greater turning force — a trade-off between speed and force that mirrors the principle of moments.

The speed ratio between two meshed gears equals the inverse ratio of their numbers of teeth:

$$\frac{\text{speed of driven gear}}{\text{speed of driving gear}} = \frac{\text{teeth on driving gear}}{\text{teeth on driven gear}}$$

A bicycle uses this principle: changing to a larger sprocket (more teeth) on the rear wheel reduces speed but increases the force applied — useful when climbing hills. The pedal gear (chainring) drives the rear sprocket. Adjacent meshed gears always rotate in opposite directions.

A driving gear has 20 teeth and rotates at 300 rpm. It meshes with a driven gear that has 60 teeth. What is the speed of the driven gear?

Speed of driven gear = (teeth on driver ÷ teeth on driven) × speed of driver
= (20 ÷ 60) × 300
= 100 rpm

The driven gear is larger and therefore rotates more slowly — but it applies three times the torque of the driving gear. The two gears also rotate in opposite directions.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Moments questions are frequently worth 3–4 marks and hinge on one mistake: students use the slant distance rather than the perpendicular distance from the pivot to the force. Always check that \(d\) in \(M = Fd\) is the perpendicular distance — if the force is applied at an angle, you must resolve it first. In 6-mark describe-a-method questions about finding the centre of mass, examiners want: suspend object freely from two different points, draw plumb lines, the intersection is the centre of mass. Missing either suspension point or the intersection step loses marks. For gear calculations, write the ratio explicitly before substituting — it prevents sign errors.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Vectors have magnitude and direction (force, velocity); scalars have magnitude only (speed, mass). Free-body diagrams show all forces on a single object as labelled arrows.
  • Moment = force × perpendicular distance (M = Fd, in N m). For equilibrium: total clockwise moments = total anticlockwise moments (principle of moments).
  • Levers use the principle of moments for mechanical advantage. Gears transmit turning forces: a small driving gear meshing a large driven gear reduces speed but increases force, in inverse proportion to tooth count.

lessons.title: Electric Circuits, Ohm's Law and I-V Characteristics
lessons.description: Charge, current, potential difference, resistance, Ohm's law, I-V graphs and the circuit core practical.
lessons.content_html:
Electric Current and Charge

Electric current is the flow of charge carriers through a conductor. In metals, these are electrons moving from the negative terminal to the positive terminal — although by convention, current direction is defined as flowing from positive to negative. In solutions (electrolytes), both positive and negative ions carry the current.

Key Fact

Charge is measured in coulombs (C). The equation linking charge, current and time is: \(Q = It\), where \(Q\) is charge in coulombs, \(I\) is current in amperes (A), and \(t\) is time in seconds. One ampere means one coulomb of charge passes a point every second.

Current is measured with an ammeter connected in series with the component. Potential difference (voltage) is measured with a voltmeter connected in parallel.

Potential Difference

Potential difference (p.d.) is the energy transferred per unit of charge that flows between two points. Think of it as the electrical 'push' that drives charge around the circuit. The unit is the volt (V): one volt means one joule of energy is transferred per coulomb of charge.

Resistance and Ohm's Law

Resistance opposes current flow. The relationship between potential difference, current and resistance is given by Ohm's law:

$$V = I \times R$$

Where \(V\) is potential difference in volts, \(I\) is current in amperes, and \(R\) is resistance in ohms (Ω). This can be rearranged: \(I = V/R\) (to find current) and \(R = V/I\) (to find resistance).

Key Fact

An ohmic conductor has a constant resistance at constant temperature. For ohmic conductors, doubling the voltage exactly doubles the current. Most metal resistors behave ohmically at room temperature.

I-V Characteristics

An I-V characteristic graph plots current (y-axis) against potential difference (x-axis). The shape of the graph reveals how resistance behaves. The core practical (Topic 10) requires you to investigate the I-V characteristics of at least a resistor and a filament lamp.

For a fixed resistor at constant temperature, the I-V graph is a straight line through the origin. This confirms that current is directly proportional to potential difference — the definition of an ohmic conductor. The gradient of the line equals \(1/R\): a steeper line means lower resistance.

The same straight-line graph applies for both positive and negative p.d. values — the resistor works the same way in both directions.

The I-V graph for a filament lamp is curved — the gradient decreases as current increases. This is because the tungsten filament heats up as more current flows: higher temperature means more resistance. The graph is symmetrical about the origin (same shape in both directions).

A diode conducts very easily in one direction (forward bias) but has an extremely high resistance in the other direction (reverse bias). Its I-V graph shows almost zero current until the forward voltage threshold is reached, then current rises steeply. In reverse bias, current is essentially zero.

LDRs and Thermistors

Two variable resistors feature prominently in circuit design and exam questions:

A light-dependent resistor (LDR) has a resistance that falls as light intensity increases. In bright conditions, resistance is low; in darkness, resistance is high. LDRs are used in automatic street lighting and camera light meters.

A thermistor (negative temperature coefficient, NTC, type) has a resistance that decreases as temperature increases. They are used in temperature sensors, thermostats, and fire alarms. In a potential-divider circuit, a thermistor can control a relay that switches a heater on or off.

Series and Parallel Circuits

In a series circuit, the same current flows through every component. Voltages add up across components. Total resistance is the sum of individual resistances: \(R_{total} = R_1 + R_2 + R_3\).

In a parallel circuit, each branch has the same potential difference across it (equal to the supply). The total current from the supply equals the sum of the branch currents. Adding more branches decreases the total resistance.

Key Fact

Series: current same everywhere; voltages add up; resistances add up. Parallel: voltage same across all branches; currents add up (junction rule); total resistance is less than the smallest individual resistance. Household appliances are wired in parallel so each receives the full supply voltage.

To plot an I-V characteristic, connect the component in series with an ammeter and a variable resistor (rheostat). Connect a voltmeter in parallel with the component. Adjust the variable resistor to vary the current through the component and record corresponding current and voltage values. Plot I (y-axis) against V (x-axis). Repeat for both polarities where relevant (e.g. a resistor — reverse the cell connections).

For the filament lamp, allow cooling time between readings, as temperature affects resistance. Record at least six evenly spaced values for a reliable graph. Repeat readings to check for anomalies.
lessons.exam_tip_html: The core practical for I-V characteristics comes up regularly in extended questions. Examiners want the method in full: variable resistor to change p.d., ammeter in series, voltmeter in parallel — state all three. For the filament lamp graph, explain the curvature: 'as current increases, the filament heats up, which increases resistance, so current does not increase in proportion to p.d.' In circuit calculations, always identify whether components are in series or parallel before choosing the right equation — many errors come from applying series rules to a parallel branch.

lessons.title: Mains Electricity, Power and the National Grid
lessons.description: AC vs DC, plug wiring and safety, power equations, and how the National Grid uses transformers efficiently.
lessons.content_html:
Alternating Current and Direct Current

Alternating current (a.c.) changes direction repeatedly. The UK mains supply is a.c. at a frequency of 50 Hz, meaning it completes 50 full cycles per second. The peak voltage of UK mains is approximately 325 V, but the declared supply voltage is 230 V — this represents the equivalent d.c. voltage that would deliver the same power.

Direct current (d.c.) flows in one direction only. Batteries and cells supply d.c. Electronic devices (phones, laptops) typically require d.c. internally; their chargers convert mains a.c. to low-voltage d.c.

Key Fact

UK mains supply: alternating current (a.c.), declared voltage 230 V, frequency 50 Hz. Batteries supply direct current (d.c.). The mains frequency of 50 Hz means the current changes direction 100 times per second (two direction changes per cycle).

The Three-Pin Plug

Most UK appliances connect to the mains through a three-pin plug. The three wires have standardised colours introduced with post-2006 wiring regulations:

Live wire (brown) — carries the alternating potential difference from the supply, alternating between approximately +325 V and −325 V relative to earth.

Neutral wire (blue) — completes the circuit. It is at, or close to, 0 V (earth potential). Current returns to the supply via this wire.

Earth wire (green and yellow) — a safety wire connected to the metal casing of an appliance. It carries current safely to earth if a fault causes the casing to become live, tripping the fuse or circuit breaker.

The live wire is at a high potential difference (∼230 V) relative to earth at all times — even when the appliance switch is off. If you touch it, a large p.d. exists between your body and the ground, driving a current through you. Switches are therefore always placed in the live wire so that when open, the appliance and the neutral/earth wires are isolated from the high-voltage supply.

Fuses and Circuit Breakers

A fuse is connected in series in the live wire. If a fault causes an excessive current to flow, the fuse wire melts, breaking the circuit before the appliance or cable can overheat and cause a fire. Fuses are rated at 3 A, 5 A, or 13 A for most domestic appliances — the fuse rating should be just above the normal operating current.

A circuit breaker serves the same protective purpose but can be reset by pressing a switch — no replacement is needed. Residual current device (RCD) circuit breakers detect tiny imbalances between live and neutral currents (indicating a leakage to earth) and trip within milliseconds — faster than a fuse melts.

Electrical Power

Electrical power is the rate of energy transfer. The fundamental equation is:

$$P = IV$$

Where \(P\) is power in watts, \(I\) is current in amperes, and \(V\) is potential difference in volts. Combining with \(V = IR\) gives two further equations:

$$P = I^2R \quad \text{and} \quad P = \frac{V^2}{R}$$

\(P = I^2R\) is particularly useful for calculating power dissipated in a resistor when you know the current; \(P = V^2/R\) when you know the voltage. On a long transmission wire, power is wasted as heat — this dissipation follows \(P_{lost} = I^2R\), showing that reducing current dramatically reduces heat losses.

Key Fact

Three power equations: \(P = IV\) (use when both current and voltage are given); \(P = I^2R\) (use when current and resistance are given); \(P = V^2/R\) (use when voltage and resistance are given). Power is always in watts; energy transferred is \(E = Pt\) in joules.

Energy Transferred

Energy transferred by an electrical device is given by:

$$E = Pt \quad \text{and also} \quad E = QV$$

Where \(E\) is energy in joules, \(P\) is power in watts, \(t\) is time in seconds, \(Q\) is charge in coulombs, and \(V\) is potential difference in volts. The equation \(E = QV\) links directly to the definition of potential difference as energy per unit charge.

A kettle operates at 230 V and draws a current of 9 A. Calculate (i) its power rating and (ii) the energy it transfers in 2 minutes.

(i) \(P = IV = 9 \times 230 = 2070\) W ≈ 2.1 kW

(ii) \(t = 2 \times 60 = 120\) s
\(E = Pt = 2070 \times 120 = 248\,400\) J ≈ 248 kJ

Check: the fuse should be rated just above 9 A — a 13 A fuse is appropriate. A 3 A fuse would melt immediately under normal operation.

The National Grid and Transformers

The National Grid transmits electricity from power stations to consumers. Because power loss in cables follows \(P = I^2R\), the key strategy is to transmit at very high voltage (and therefore very low current) to minimise energy waste as heat in the cables.

A transformer uses electromagnetic induction to change the voltage of an a.c. supply. Transformers work only with a.c. — this is one reason the National Grid uses a.c. rather than d.c.

A step-up transformer at the power station increases voltage from around 25 kV to 132 kV, 275 kV, or 400 kV for long-distance transmission. At the end of the transmission line, a series of step-down transformers reduce the voltage progressively to 33 kV, then 11 kV, then 230 V for domestic use.

Key Fact

High-voltage transmission keeps current low, which reduces power lost as heat in cables (\(P_{lost} = I^2R\)). A step-up transformer increases voltage at the power station; step-down transformers reduce it before it reaches homes.

A transformer works because the changing magnetic field produced by alternating current in the primary coil induces an alternating voltage in the secondary coil. A steady (d.c.) current produces a constant magnetic field — no change, no induction, no output voltage. This is why the National Grid must use a.c.: only a.c. allows transformers to step voltage up or down efficiently.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Plug wiring is tested every year — memorise: brown = live, blue = neutral, green/yellow = earth. The most common error is stating the fuse is in the neutral wire: it is always in the live wire. For National Grid questions, the key explanation is always: high voltage → low current → less power wasted (\(P = I^2R\)). For 6-mark extended responses, link each step explicitly: power station → step-up transformer → high-voltage cables → step-down substation → homes. State the equation and say what each variable does. On power calculations, choose the right equation for the information given — if current and resistance are given, use \(P = I^2R\) directly rather than finding V first.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • UK mains is a.c. at 230 V, 50 Hz. Plug wires: live (brown), neutral (blue), earth (green/yellow). Fuse in the live wire. Batteries supply d.c.
  • Three power equations: \(P = IV\), \(P = I^2R\), \(P = V^2/R\). Energy transferred: \(E = Pt\) and \(E = QV\).
  • The National Grid uses step-up transformers at power stations (high voltage, low current) to minimise \(I^2R\) losses during transmission. Step-down transformers reduce voltage to 230 V for domestic use. Transformers only work with a.c.

lessons.title: Static Electricity and Electric Fields
lessons.description: How insulators charge by friction, electrostatic attraction and repulsion, dangers, and electric fields.
lessons.content_html:
Charging by Friction

When two insulating materials are rubbed together, electrons transfer from one material to the other. The material that gains electrons becomes negatively charged; the material that loses electrons becomes positively charged. The total charge is conserved — charge is not created, only redistributed.

A classic example: rubbing a polythene rod with a cloth causes electrons to transfer from the cloth to the polythene. The rod gains a negative charge; the cloth becomes positive. Rubbing an acetate rod with a cloth has the opposite effect — electrons transfer from the acetate to the cloth, leaving the rod positive.

Key Fact

Only electrons transfer when charging by friction — protons are locked inside atomic nuclei and cannot move in ordinary chemical processes. The object that gains electrons becomes negative; the object that loses them becomes positive. Total charge before equals total charge after.

Attraction and Repulsion

Charged objects exert forces on one another without touching — this is an electrostatic (non-contact) force. The rule is:

Like charges repel; unlike charges attract.

Two negatively charged rods brought close together will push each other away. A negative rod held near a positive rod will pull each other towards the other. These forces act at a distance because each charged object creates an electric field around itself.

Charged objects also attract small uncharged objects — for example, a charged comb attracting small pieces of paper. This happens because the charge on the comb induces a redistribution of charge in the paper, attracting the opposite charges on the near side.

Electric Fields

An electric field is the region around a charged object in which a force acts on another charged object. Electric fields are represented using electric field lines. The rules are:

  • Field lines run from positive to negative (the direction a positive charge would move).
  • Field lines never cross each other.
  • The closer together the field lines, the stronger the field.
  • For a uniform field (between two parallel plates), the lines are parallel and evenly spaced.

Around an isolated positive charge, field lines radiate outward in all directions (like the spokes of a wheel). Around a negative charge, they point inward toward the charge. Between two oppositely charged parallel plates, the field lines are parallel, equally spaced, and perpendicular to the plates — this is a uniform field. The field is stronger close to the plates and weaker at the edges (edge effects).

Earthing and Electrostatic Hazards

Earthing removes charge from an object by providing a conducting path to the ground. Since the Earth is very large, it can accept or provide huge numbers of electrons without becoming noticeably charged itself.

Electrostatic charge is a hazard in several situations. Sparks occur when the electric field between a charged object and earth becomes strong enough to ionise the air — the resulting spark can ignite flammable vapours. This is why aircraft are earthed before refuelling: fuel flowing through pipes builds up static charge, and without earthing, a spark could ignite aviation fuel vapour.

Surgeons in operating theatres and workers handling explosive materials wear special anti-static clothing and footwear to prevent charge build-up. Computer components are stored in anti-static bags because even a small static discharge can damage integrated circuits.

Key Fact

Electrostatic hazards arise wherever charge can accumulate and spark: aircraft refuelling (earth the aircraft before attaching fuel hose), operating theatres (anti-static clothing), grain silos and flour mills (dust clouds are explosive — anti-static earthing). Lightning itself is a large-scale electrostatic discharge.

Useful Applications of Static Electricity

Static electricity also has many practical applications:

Electrostatic paint spraying: The object to be painted (e.g. a car body panel) is given one charge; the paint droplets are given the opposite charge. The paint is attracted to every surface of the object, including awkward recesses, giving an even coat and reducing waste.

Inkjet printers: Tiny ink droplets are given a charge as they leave the nozzle. Deflector plates with a controlled electric field steer each droplet to exactly the right position on the page.

Photocopiers and laser printers: A drum is given a static charge pattern representing the image to be printed. Toner (charged powder) is attracted to the charged regions of the drum and then transferred to paper.

Electrostatic precipitators: Used in power station chimneys, these give particles in smoke a charge so they are attracted to collecting plates, removing them from the exhaust gas and reducing air pollution.

In a thundercloud, turbulent air movements cause ice crystals and water droplets to collide, transferring charge. The base of the cloud typically accumulates a large negative charge, while the ground below becomes induced into a positive charge. When the potential difference between cloud and ground becomes large enough, the air ionises and an enormous discharge — lightning — occurs. Lightning conductors on tall buildings provide a low-resistance earthing path, protecting the building by allowing the charge to discharge safely into the ground rather than through the structure.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For static electricity questions, the most common error is writing that 'positive charges move' — in solids, it is always electrons that transfer. Always state 'electrons transfer from X to Y.' For electric field line diagrams, check: lines go from positive to negative; they never cross; closer lines mean stronger field. In application questions (paint spraying, inkjet printers), explain the principle, not just the fact — 'opposite charges attract, so every surface of the object is reached' earns more marks than 'the paint sticks to the car.' For 6-mark extended responses on hazards, structure your answer: state the hazard → explain why charge builds up → explain how the spark is caused → state the control measure.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Charging by friction transfers electrons only (not protons). The material gaining electrons becomes negative; the material losing electrons becomes positive. Like charges repel; unlike charges attract.
  • Electric fields surround charged objects. Field lines point from positive to negative; closer lines mean a stronger field. A uniform field exists between parallel plates with opposite charges.
  • Electrostatic hazards (sparks near fuel, operating theatres, grain dust) are managed by earthing. Applications include electrostatic paint spraying, inkjet printers, photocopiers and electrostatic precipitators.

lessons.title: Magnetism, Electromagnets and the Motor Effect
lessons.description: Permanent and induced magnets, solenoids, Fleming's left-hand rule, F = BIl and the motor effect.
lessons.content_html:
Permanent and Induced Magnets

A permanent magnet produces its own magnetic field at all times. It always has a north pole and a south pole. Like poles repel each other; unlike poles attract. Common magnetic materials include iron, steel, nickel, and cobalt.

An induced magnet is a material that becomes temporarily magnetic when placed inside a magnetic field. When removed, it quickly loses its magnetism. An induced magnet is always attracted to the permanent magnet that induced it — it is never repelled, because its poles align with the external field.

Key Fact

A magnetic field is the space in which a magnetic force acts. Outside a bar magnet, field lines run from the north pole to the south pole. Denser (closer) field lines indicate a stronger field. The Earth has its own magnetic field — a compass needle aligns with this field to point approximately north.

Place a small plotting compass near a bar magnet. Mark where the needle points. Move the compass so the rear of the needle is at your mark, then mark the new needle tip position. Repeat to trace the full field line. Alternatively, place the magnet under paper and sprinkle iron filings on top — the filings align with the field, revealing its pattern.

Electromagnetism

When an electric current flows through a wire, it creates a magnetic field around the wire. The field lines form concentric circles around the wire. Reversing the current reverses the field direction. Increasing the current increases the field strength.

A solenoid is a coil of wire. When current flows through it, the field inside the solenoid is strong and nearly uniform, with a pattern similar to a bar magnet — one end acts as a north pole and the other as a south pole. The field strength increases if you: increase the current, increase the number of turns per unit length, or insert an iron core.

Key Fact

An electromagnet is a solenoid with a soft iron core. The core concentrates the magnetic field. Switching off the current removes the magnetism — this controllability makes electromagnets useful in scrapyard cranes (lifting/releasing scrap metal), circuit breakers, electric bells, and MRI scanners.

The Motor Effect

When a current-carrying wire is placed inside a magnetic field, it experiences a force. This is called the motor effect. The force is at its maximum when the wire is perpendicular to the magnetic field lines, and zero when the wire is parallel to them.

Reversing either the current direction or the magnetic field direction reverses the force. Reversing both leaves the force in the same direction.

Fleming's Left-Hand Rule

Fleming's left-hand rule gives the direction of the motor-effect force. Hold your left hand with the thumb, index finger, and middle finger at right angles to each other:

  • Index finger — direction of the magnetic field (north to south).
  • Middle finger — direction of conventional current (positive to negative).
  • Thumb — direction of the force (thrust/motion) on the wire.

The size of the force on a current-carrying wire in a magnetic field is given by:

$$F = BIl$$

Where \(F\) is force in newtons (N), \(B\) is magnetic flux density in tesla (T), \(I\) is current in amperes (A), and \(l\) is the length of wire within the magnetic field in metres (m). This equation assumes the wire is perpendicular to the field.

Worked example: A wire of length 0.15 m carries a current of 4 A in a magnetic field of flux density 0.5 T. The wire is perpendicular to the field. Find the force on the wire.
\(F = BIl = 0.5 \times 4 \times 0.15 = 0.3\) N

The DC Motor

A simple d.c. motor uses the motor effect to produce rotation. A rectangular coil of wire sits between the poles of a permanent magnet. When current flows through the coil, the motor-effect force pushes one side of the coil up and the other side down. This creates a turning force that rotates the coil.

After the coil has rotated 180°, the sides that were being pushed up and down swap positions. Without a correction, the forces would now act in the opposite rotational direction and the coil would stop. A split-ring commutator solves this: as the coil reaches the vertical position, the two halves of the split ring swap which brush contact they touch, automatically reversing the current in the coil. This means the force direction is maintained and the coil continues to spin in the same direction.

The speed of a d.c. motor can be increased by: increasing the current through the coil, increasing the magnetic flux density (using a stronger magnet), or increasing the number of turns on the coil.

Key Fact

The split-ring commutator reverses the current through the coil every half-turn. Without it, the motor-effect force would reverse direction after 180° and the coil would oscillate rather than rotate continuously. This makes it the critical component enabling one-direction rotation in a d.c. motor.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Fleming's left-hand rule questions always require you to state which finger represents which quantity — don't assume the examiner knows you know. For F = BIl calculations, check the unit of B is in tesla before substituting, and confirm the wire is stated to be perpendicular to the field (if not, the equation doesn't directly apply). A very common error in motor questions is forgetting the split-ring commutator: many students explain why the coil starts rotating but don't explain why it keeps rotating. Always finish with: 'the commutator reverses the current every half-turn, maintaining the same rotational direction.' For 6-mark extended responses on the motor, a logical sequence earns top marks: current in coil → motor-effect force → rotation → commutator → continuous rotation.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Permanent magnets have a persistent field; induced magnets are temporary (always attracted, never repelled). A current-carrying wire creates a magnetic field; a solenoid with an iron core is an electromagnet.
  • The motor effect: a force acts on a current-carrying wire in a magnetic field. Fleming's left-hand rule gives the direction. The force F = BIl (tesla × amperes × metres).
  • A d.c. motor uses the motor effect; the split-ring commutator reverses current every half-turn to maintain continuous rotation in one direction.

lessons.title: Electromagnetic Induction and Transformers
lessons.description: Generator effect, microphones, transformers, turns-ratio and power equations.
lessons.content_html:
Electromagnetic Induction

When a conductor moves through a magnetic field — or when a magnetic field changes around a stationary conductor — a electromagnetic induction occurs. The result is an induced electromotive force (EMF). If the conductor forms part of a closed circuit, this EMF drives a current. If the circuit is open, only a voltage appears across the ends of the conductor.

Three factors control how large the induced EMF is. Moving the conductor faster increases the rate at which field lines are cut, so the induced EMF rises. Using a stronger magnet increases the field strength, again boosting the EMF. Adding more turns to a coil multiplies the effect because each turn contributes its own induced EMF. Reversing the direction of motion — or reversing the magnet — reverses the direction of the induced current.

Key Fact

Increasing the speed of motion, the magnetic field strength, or the number of coil turns all increase the induced EMF. Reversing the motion reverses the current direction.

The Generator Effect

The generator effect is used in every electrical generator. In an alternator, a coil rotates continuously inside a magnetic field. As the coil spins, the angle between the coil and the field lines changes constantly, so the rate of cutting field lines changes too. This produces an alternating voltage — one that regularly reverses direction — which is the basis of the alternating current (AC) supplied to homes and businesses.

A dynamo uses a similar rotating coil but includes a split-ring commutator. This device swaps the connections to the external circuit every half-turn, so the output voltage always points the same way. The result is a pulsating direct current (DC) rather than a smooth AC output.

Microphones and Loudspeakers

A dynamic microphone converts sound into an electrical signal using the generator effect. A thin diaphragm is attached to a coil of wire sitting inside a permanent magnet. When sound waves reach the microphone, the diaphragm vibrates, moving the coil back and forth in the magnetic field. This motion induces a varying EMF that mirrors the pattern of the sound wave.

A loudspeaker works in reverse: an alternating current through a coil in a magnetic field creates a varying force (by the motor effect), which vibrates the cone and produces sound. The pair — microphone and loudspeaker — demonstrates how electrical and mechanical energy convert back and forth via electromagnetic principles.

Transformers

A transformer changes the voltage of an AC supply. It consists of a primary coil and a secondary coil, both wound around a shared iron core. When alternating current flows in the primary coil, it creates a constantly changing magnetic field in the iron core. This changing field passes through the secondary coil and induces an alternating EMF in it — the process of mutual induction.

The iron core is chosen because it is easily magnetised and demagnetised many times per second, allowing it to carry the changing magnetic field efficiently between the coils. The coils are electrically insulated from each other and from the core, so there is no direct electrical connection — energy is transferred entirely by the changing magnetic field.

Key Fact

The turns-ratio equation links the voltages and numbers of turns in a transformer:

$$\frac{V_p}{V_s} = \frac{N_p}{N_s}$$

where \(V_p\) is the primary voltage, \(V_s\) is the secondary voltage, \(N_p\) is the number of primary turns, and \(N_s\) is the number of secondary turns.

Step-Up and Step-Down Transformers

A step-up transformer has more turns on the secondary coil than the primary coil (\(N_s > N_p\)), so the output voltage is higher than the input. A step-down transformer has fewer turns on the secondary (\(N_s < N_p\)), so it reduces the voltage. The ratio of turns equals the ratio of voltages.

Question: A transformer has 500 turns on its primary coil and 50 turns on its secondary. The primary voltage is 230 V. Calculate the secondary voltage.

Step 1 — Write the equation:

$$\frac{V_p}{V_s} = \frac{N_p}{N_s}$$

Step 2 — Substitute:

$$\frac{230}{V_s} = \frac{500}{50}$$

Step 3 — Rearrange and solve:

$$V_s = \frac{230 \times 50}{500} = 23 \text{ V}$$

This is a step-down transformer — 10 times fewer secondary turns means 10 times lower output voltage.

Power and Efficiency in Transformers

For a transformer assumed to be 100% efficient (no energy losses), the power delivered to the primary coil equals the power output from the secondary coil. Since power equals voltage multiplied by current, this gives the power equation:

$$V_p I_p = V_s I_s$$

This equation reveals an important consequence: when a step-up transformer increases voltage, the current must decrease by the same factor. If voltage doubles, current halves. This trade-off is why high-voltage transmission saves energy, as explored in the next section.

Question: A step-up transformer has 400 turns on the primary and 8,000 turns on the secondary. The primary voltage is 25 V and the primary current is 4.0 A. Assuming 100% efficiency, calculate (a) the secondary voltage and (b) the secondary current.

Part (a) — Secondary voltage using turns-ratio:

$$\frac{25}{V_s} = \frac{400}{8000} \Rightarrow V_s = \frac{25 \times 8000}{400} = 500 \text{ V}$$

Part (b) — Secondary current using power equation:

$$V_p I_p = V_s I_s \Rightarrow 25 \times 4.0 = 500 \times I_s$$

$$I_s = \frac{100}{500} = 0.20 \text{ A}$$

The current fell from 4.0 A to 0.20 A — a factor of 20, matching the voltage increase.

The National Grid and Transmission Losses

Electricity generated at a power station is transmitted across the country through the National Grid — a network of cables connecting power stations to homes, schools, and businesses. Cables have electrical resistance, and whenever current flows through a resistor, energy is lost as heat. The power lost in a cable is given by:

$$P_{\text{loss}} = I^2 R$$

Because power loss depends on the square of the current, even a modest reduction in current produces a dramatic reduction in energy wasted. Doubling the voltage halves the current, which reduces the cable losses to one quarter. This is why the National Grid transmits electricity at very high voltages — typically hundreds of thousands of volts — for long-distance transmission.

At the power station, a step-up transformer raises the generated voltage to this high transmission voltage. Near consumers, step-down transformers progressively reduce the voltage to the safe levels used in homes (230 V) and industry. The whole system depends on the fact that transformers only work with alternating current.

Real transformers are not perfectly efficient. Energy is lost as heat in the resistance of the coils and through eddy currents induced in the iron core. Modern transformer designs — using laminated cores to reduce eddy currents — achieve efficiencies above 99%, making the losses very small in practice.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Transformer calculations are common in this unit. For turns-ratio questions, always write \(V_p/V_s = N_p/N_s\) before substituting — do not try to shortcut with mental arithmetic. For questions with both a voltage and a current unknown, you need both equations in sequence: turns-ratio first to find the missing voltage, then \(V_p I_p = V_s I_s\) for the current. The power equation only applies when the question states 100% efficiency or “no energy losses.” Always state your units in the final answer — forgetting V or A costs the mark.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Electromagnetic induction produces a voltage whenever a conductor experiences a changing magnetic field; the size of the EMF depends on speed, field strength, and number of turns.
  • Transformers use mutual induction to change AC voltages: \(V_p/V_s = N_p/N_s\), and at 100% efficiency \(V_p I_p = V_s I_s\).
  • High-voltage transmission across the National Grid reduces the current and therefore the \(I^2 R\) energy losses in the cables; step-up and step-down transformers make this possible.

lessons.title: Particle Model: Density, States and the Gas Laws
lessons.description: States, density core practical, specific heat capacity, latent heat and Boyle's law.
lessons.content_html:
States of Matter and the Particle Model

The particle model explains the properties of solids, liquids, and gases in terms of particle spacing, movement, and the forces between particles. In a solid, particles are arranged in a regular lattice and can only vibrate; they cannot change position. In a liquid, particles are still close together but can move past one another, which is why liquids flow and take the shape of their container. In a gas, particles are far apart and move quickly in all directions, filling whatever space is available.

When a substance changes state — for example from solid to liquid on melting — energy must be supplied to overcome the forces (bonds) between particles. The particles gain potential energy as they separate, but their kinetic energy — and therefore the temperature — does not rise during the change of state. This is why a temperature–time graph shows a flat plateau while a substance is changing state, even though heat is still being added.

Density

Density describes how much mass is packed into a given volume. The equation is:

$$\rho = \frac{m}{V}$$

where \(\rho\) is density (kg/m³ or g/cm³), \(m\) is mass (kg or g), and \(V\) is volume (m³ or cm³). Solids are generally denser than liquids, and liquids are much denser than gases, because the particles are more closely packed. Water has a density of 1,000 kg/m³ (or 1.0 g/cm³); any object less dense than water will float in it.

Key Fact

Density equation: \(\rho = m/V\). For a regular solid (cuboid, cylinder), calculate volume from dimensions. For an irregular solid, use the displacement method: submerge it in a measuring cylinder of water and read off the volume of water displaced.

Core Practical: Measuring Density

This core practical requires you to measure the density of both regular and irregular solids and liquids. For a regular solid such as a rectangular block, use a ruler to measure length, width, and height, then calculate volume (length × width × height). Use a balance to measure mass. Then apply \(\rho = m/V\).

For an irregular solid, fill a measuring cylinder with water to a known level and record this volume. Carefully lower the solid into the water and record the new water level. The difference between the two readings equals the volume of the solid. This method is sometimes called the displacement method or the Eureka can method when a displacement can is used instead.

For a liquid, measure the mass of an empty container on a balance, then add the liquid and measure the combined mass. Subtract to find the mass of the liquid. Pour the liquid into a measuring cylinder to find its volume. Calculate \(\rho = m/V\).

Question: A student immerses a stone in a measuring cylinder. The water level rises from 40.0 cm³ to 55.5 cm³. The stone has a mass of 42.0 g. Calculate the density of the stone in g/cm³.

Step 1 — Find the volume of the stone:

$$V = 55.5 - 40.0 = 15.5 \text{ cm}^3$$

Step 2 — Apply the density equation:

$$\rho = \frac{42.0}{15.5} = 2.71 \text{ g/cm}^3$$

The density is approximately 2.71 g/cm³, consistent with a granite-type rock.

Internal Energy, Specific Heat Capacity and Latent Heat

The internal energy of a substance is the total kinetic and potential energy of all its particles. When you heat a substance, you increase its internal energy. If the substance is not changing state, the extra energy goes into increasing the kinetic energy of the particles, which we measure as a rise in temperature. The equation is:

$$Q = mc\Delta\theta$$

where \(Q\) is the energy transferred (J), \(m\) is mass (kg), \(c\) is the specific heat capacity (J/kg°C), and \(\Delta\theta\) is the temperature change (°C or K). Water has a specific heat capacity of 4,200 J/kg°C — much higher than most metals — which is why it is used as a coolant and in central heating systems.

The core practical for specific heat capacity (core practical 14.11) involves measuring the temperature change of water as it is heated by an electric immersion heater, recording a temperature–time graph. The same experiment is extended to observe melting ice — showing the flat plateau on the graph where energy is absorbed without a temperature change.

Key Fact

During a change of state, energy is transferred but temperature stays constant. This energy is called specific latent heat:

$$Q = mL$$

where \(L\) is the specific latent heat (J/kg). Latent heat of fusion applies to melting/freezing; latent heat of vaporisation applies to boiling/condensation.

Question: A 2.0 kg block of iron is heated from 20°C to 70°C. The specific heat capacity of iron is 450 J/kg°C. Calculate the energy transferred to the iron.

Step 1 — Find the temperature change:

$$\Delta\theta = 70 - 20 = 50 \text{ °C}$$

Step 2 — Apply Q = mcΔθ:

$$Q = 2.0 \times 450 \times 50 = 45{,}000 \text{ J}$$

The energy transferred is 45,000 J (or 45 kJ). Check: mass in kg, temperature change in °C — both correct, so units give J.

Gas Pressure and the Kinetic Theory

Gas pressure arises because gas particles are constantly moving and colliding with the walls of their container. Each collision exerts a small force on the wall, and the combined effect of billions of collisions per second creates the pressure we measure. If the temperature rises, the particles move faster and hit the walls harder and more often — so pressure increases. If the volume decreases (particles squashed into a smaller space), the particles collide with the walls more frequently — so pressure again increases.

Absolute Zero and the Kelvin Scale

Absolute zero is −273°C. At this temperature, particles would have no kinetic energy and gas pressure would drop to zero. The Kelvin scale uses absolute zero as its starting point: 0 K = −273°C. To convert from Celsius to Kelvin, add 273: \(T(\text{K}) = \theta(\text{°C}) + 273\).

Boyle's Law

For a fixed mass of gas at constant temperature, pressure and volume are inversely proportional. This relationship is Boyle's law:

$$p_1 V_1 = p_2 V_2$$

The kinetic model explains Boyle’s law: compressing the gas into a smaller volume means particles collide with the walls more often per second (shorter distances between collisions), so the pressure rises. Temperature is constant, so particle speed — and therefore force per collision — is unchanged.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For density questions, always check your units before substituting — mixing kg with cm³ gives a meaningless answer. For Q = mcΔθ, remember \(\Delta\theta\) is the change in temperature, not the final temperature. For Boyle’s law (Higher), state the conditions — “fixed mass, constant temperature” — before applying \(p_1 V_1 = p_2 V_2\); examiners credit this explicitly in 3-mark questions. When asked to explain why temperature stays constant during melting, use particle language: energy breaks bonds between particles rather than increasing their kinetic energy.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The particle model explains density (\(\rho = m/V\)), changes of state (energy breaks bonds without raising temperature), and gas pressure (particle collisions on container walls).
  • Energy for temperature changes uses \(Q = mc\Delta\theta\); energy for changes of state (at constant temperature) uses \(Q = mL\).
  • For a fixed mass of gas at constant temperature, Boyle’s law gives \(p_1 V_1 = p_2 V_2\): compressing the gas raises the pressure proportionally.

glossary_terms.definition: A scientific model that describes matter as made up of tiny particles whose arrangement and movement determine the properties of the substance.
A state of matter where particles are closely packed in a regular arrangement and vibrate about fixed positions.
A state of matter where particles are close together but can flow past each other, giving a fixed volume but no fixed shape.
A state of matter where particles are widely spaced, move rapidly and randomly, and exert negligible forces on each other.
The mass per unit volume of a substance, measured in kg/m³ or g/cm³.
The energy required to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1°C (or 1 K), measured in J/kg°C.
The energy absorbed or released by a substance when it changes state at constant temperature.
The energy per unit mass required to change the state of a substance at constant temperature, measured in J/kg.
The theoretical lowest possible temperature, −273°C (or 0 K), at which particles have minimum kinetic energy.
The force exerted per unit area on the walls of a container by collisions from gas particles, measured in pascals (Pa).
The law stating that for a fixed mass of gas at constant temperature, pressure multiplied by volume is constant: p₁V₁ = p₂V₂.
